lead: An array multiplier makes every partial product at the same time. Each bit of the multiplier opens a row of AND gates, and each row is the multiplicand shifted by that bit's place. Full adders then combine the rows at fixed columns, with carries moving diagonally down the array. The answer appears after one long ripple through the diagonals. Braun does this for unsigned numbers. Baugh-Wooley does it for two's complement by inverting the mixed sign partial products and adding two fixed 1 bits. Small embedded multipliers and many hardware interview questions still use these arrays.
prereq: You need: Chapter 4.1 for the full adder, and Chapter 4.2 for why saving carries helps when many rows must be added.

sections.h3: Rows of AND gates, added by place value

blocks.text: Write the multiplicand as A = a<sub>n−1</sub>...a<sub>0</sub> and the multiplier as B = b<sub>n−1</sub>...b<sub>0</sub>. Each bit a<sub>i</sub> and b<sub>j</sub> is 0 or 1, and n is the word length. Unsigned multiplication is shift and add. Multiplying by b<sub>j</sub>2<sup>j</sup> either adds A<<j or adds zero. The array does all these additions together.
Here P is the 2n-bit product; a<sub>i</sub> is bit i of A; b<sub>j</sub> is bit j of B; pp<sub>ij</sub> = a<sub>i</sub>b<sub>j</sub> is one partial product bit; 2<sup>i+j</sup> fixes its column.

A 4×4 array needs 16 AND gates to form pp<sub>00</sub> to pp<sub>33</sub>. It needs n(n−1) = 4×3 = 12 adder cells to reduce the four rows. Cells with no carry to take in are half adders: in the usual layout n cells are half adders and n(n−2) are full adders, so a 4×4 array has 8 full adders and 4 half adders. The first row is not added to anything, so it enters the array directly. Carries do not run along a row; each carry moves one row down and one column to the left, into the next higher weight. The last row is a ripple adder that delivers the top product bits.

The Braun multiplier is the plain unsigned array just described. Row j is A AND b<sub>j</sub>, shifted left by j. Row 0 has no shift. Row 1 is shifted one place, row 2 two places, and so on. Each adder cell adds the partial product bit that lands on it, the sum coming down from the row above, and the carry from the next lower column of the row above. The array is rectangular and regular, so it maps cleanly to a cell library and a compact layout.

items: Gate count: n<sup>2</sup> AND gates and n(n−1) adder cells, n(n−2) full adders and n half adders. A 4×4 Braun array has 16 AND gates, 8 full adders and 4 half adders.
Critical path: the slowest signal enters near the top and travels down the diagonal carry chain, then across the last row. It grows with n, not with n<sup>2</sup>.
No correction terms: every partial product is used exactly as generated. Braun is unsigned only.

blocks.text: A first delay estimate: the slowest signal passes about n − 1 adders down the rows and about n − 1 adders along the final ripple row, so t<sub>p</sub> ≈ t<sub>AND</sub> + 2(n−1)·t<sub>FA</sub>, where t<sub>FA</sub> is one adder delay. For n = 4 that is t<sub>AND</sub> + 6t<sub>FA</sub>. Wire delay and gate sizing matter in a real layout (see delay estimation and logical effort). Some syllabi ask only for the block diagram and the partial product array, not this estimate.

Signed numbers use two's complement. For an n-bit number, A = −a<sub>n−1</sub>2<sup>n−1</sup> + Σ<sub>i=0</sub><sup>n−2</sup> a<sub>i</sub>2<sup>i</sup>. The top bit has weight −2<sup>n−1</sup>, not +2<sup>n−1</sup>. If you sign-extend both inputs to 2n bits and use a Braun array, the array becomes larger and the sign bits create long rows of copies. Baugh-Wooley keeps the n×n array and corrects the sign inside it.

Generate the low bits normally: a<sub>i</sub>b<sub>j</sub> for i,j ≤ n−2. For a partial product with exactly one sign bit, use the inverted bit: NOT(a<sub>n−1</sub>b<sub>j</sub>) for j ≤ n−2, and NOT(a<sub>i</sub>b<sub>n−1</sub>) for i ≤ n−2. Keep the corner a<sub>n−1</sub>b<sub>n−1</sub> unchanged. Then add two 1 bits at fixed positions: bit n and bit 2n−1. In modulo 2<sup>2n</sup> arithmetic, these two 1s are the correction constant 2<sup>n</sup> + 2<sup>2n−1</sup>.
Here P<sub>BW</sub> is the signed product modulo 2<sup>2n</sup>; NOT(x) is 1−x; the two added powers are the two 1 bits; all powers of 2 are bit positions in the final product.

Baugh-Wooley needs (n−1)<sup>2</sup> + 1 AND gates, 2(n−1) NAND gates for the mixed sign bits, two constant 1 inputs and about n(n−1) adder cells. It avoids a separate sign-fix adder and avoids sign extension rows. The array topology and diagonal carry path stay the same as Braun, so the delay is still dominated by the diagonal carry. The saving is area and regularity, not a shorter critical path.

spec.aria: Partial product grid for 1101 times 1011: rows 1101 shifted by 0, 1 and 3 places and a zero row, summing to 10001111.

examples.question: Multiply a = 1101₂ (13) by b = 1011₂ (11) on a 4×4 Braun array. Show every partial product row, its place value, the sum, and the final 8-bit product.
steps: Read the multiplier bits from LSB: b0=1, b1=1, b2=0, b3=1.
Row for b0=1: A×1 = 1101₂ = 13. Place value 2⁰ = 1, so it contributes 13.
examples.check:
a = int('1101', 2)
b = int('1011', 2)
rows = []
for j in range(4):
    bit = (b >> j) & 1
    rows.append((a * bit) << j)
print(a)
print(b)
for r in rows:
    print(r)
print(sum(rows))
print(a*b)

examples.question: Read the same bit patterns as 4-bit two's complement numbers: a = 1101 (−3) and b = 1011 (−5). Multiply them with a Baugh-Wooley array. Show each row with its inverted bits, add the two correction 1s at bit 4 and bit 7, and read the 8-bit product.
steps: Bits: a₀ = 1, a₁ = 0, a₂ = 1, a₃ = 1; b₀ = 1, b₁ = 1, b₂ = 0, b₃ = 1. Sign bits are a₃ and b₃.
Row b₀ (weights 3 to 0): NOT(a₃b₀) = NOT(1) = 0, a₂b₀ = 1, a₁b₀ = 0, a₀b₀ = 1, so 0101 = 5.
Row b₁ (weights 4 to 1): NOT(a₃b₁) = 0, a₂b₁ = 1, a₁b₁ = 0, a₀b₁ = 1, so 01010 = 10.
Row b₂ (weights 5 to 2): b₂ = 0, so the three plain bits are 0 and NOT(a₃b₂) = NOT(0) = 1 at weight 5: value 32.
Row b₃ (weights 6 to 3): corner a₃b₃ = 1 at weight 6 stays plain; NOT(a₂b₃) = 0, NOT(a₁b₃) = 1, NOT(a₀b₃) = 0, so 1010 at weights 6 to 3: value 80.
examples.answer: The product is 00001111₂ = +15. The same bits read as unsigned gave 143 in worked example 1; Baugh-Wooley gets the signed answer from the same-sized array.

traps: In Braun, adding the partial products without their place-value shifts. Row 1 is shifted one place, not added as the same weight as row 0.
In Baugh-Wooley, dropping the two correction 1 bits, or inverting the corner a<sub>n−1</sub>b<sub>n−1</sub>. The corner has a positive weight and stays normal.
Inverting every sign-bit row completely. Only partial products with exactly one sign bit are inverted; the corner is the exception.
Mixing the counts: an n×n array has n<sup>2</sup> AND gates and n(n−1) adder cells (n(n−2) full adders and n half adders), not n<sup>2</sup> full adders.
Assuming array delay is n<sup>2</sup> gate delays. The critical path is the diagonal carry plus the final ripple, roughly linear in n.

quiz.q: For an n×n Braun array, how many AND gates, full adders and half adders are used?
quiz.a: n² AND gates and n(n−1) adder cells: n(n−2) full adders and n half adders. For n = 4: 16 AND gates, 8 full adders and 4 half adders.

quiz.q: Why do the carries in an array multiplier move diagonally instead of along one row?
quiz.a: Each partial product row is shifted by one column. A carry out of column k in row j has weight 2<sup>k+1</sup> and must enter column k+1 of the next row. That next row is shifted, so the carry path steps one row down and one column to the left, towards the higher weights.

quiz.q: Use a 4×4 Braun array to multiply a = 1010₂ (10) by b = 0110₂ (6). List the four rows and the product.
In Baugh-Wooley, why is the corner partial product a<sub>n−1</sub>b<sub>n−1</sub> not inverted while the other sign-bit partial products are inverted?
quiz.a: The corner term has weight +2<sup>2n−2</sup> in the signed expansion, because negative times negative is positive. The mixed terms have negative weights. Inverting the mixed AND terms and adding 2<sup>n</sup> + 2<sup>2n−1</sup> turns those negatives into valid positive array bits. Inverting the corner would remove the positive term and break the correction.

quiz.q: For a 6×6 Baugh-Wooley multiplier, give the number of partial product bits, adder cells, and mixed sign partial products that are inverted.
quiz.a: n = 6: n² = 36 partial product bits; n(n−1) = 30 adder cells; 2(n−1) = 10 mixed sign bits are inverted (NAND gates), leaving 26 plain AND gates.

quiz.q: What correction bits does an n×n Baugh-Wooley array add?
quiz.a: Two 1 bits, at bit positions n and 2n−1.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real chips rarely use a bare array for wide multiplication; they combine Booth recoding, a Wallace tree, and a fast final adder. The Baugh-Wooley idea still appears inside signed multipliers and in hardware interview questions. Search next for "Baugh-Wooley multiplier array" and "array multiplier critical path".
